reviews.title: No, I will not give you my phone number
reviews.text: Through a web search, I came across a post I thought I might enjoy reading and there was an offer to “claim your free post.” So I entered my email. Little did I know I would then be required to download the app. Why couldn’t I just do this on the computer? I hate reading on a phone and I don’t want yet another app filling up my phone’s storage and screen. But I did it anyway and listed my interests as required. Then it dumped me in the middle of things and I had to find my way back to the post that interested me to begin with and claim the post. At this point, it wouldn’t let me read the post without “verifying” my phone number. You already have my email. You already wormed your way onto the phone itself. You don’t need my number. You don’t need another piece of my data that can get hacked. You don’t need to invade my privacy. Reading the one post was not worth it. I’ll be deleting the app after posting this review. There’s enough to read out there without giving away my number. (Also, if you read through the positive reviews here, you’ll find that many of them are about the writers that user is reading, not the app itself.)

reviews.title: Algorithm problem
reviews.text: The issue I have a Substack that you can spend days if not weeks writing in an incredible article but because they’re algorithm isn’t sophisticated enough, your article won’t make it to people who are interested in reading about the things that you write about. After six months of pumping our articles every week I got tired of very few people looking at my work. I’ve had one article that seems to be pushing through the algorithm like Crazy with over 2000 likes but every other article I’ve written just doesn’t get pushed to the right crowd. I think I’ll reuse it when they change their algorithm software.

reviews.title: Una plataforma para escritores con un editor vergonzosamente desastrosa
reviews.text:
Resulta incomprensible que una plataforma dedicada a la escritura y publicación de artículos ofrezca una experiencia de edición tan frustrante, ineficiente y extraordinariamente rudimentaria.

Aplicar formato a un título, destacar una frase o insertar una cita puede requerir tres o cuatro intentos para conseguir que el editor responda correctamente. Lo que debería ser una operación sencilla termina convirtiéndose en una batalla constante contra la propia aplicación. Cada párrafo exige un esfuerzo innecesario y una paciencia que ningún usuario debería verse obligado a tener.

Un trabajo editorial que normalmente tomaría una hora puede terminar consumiendo tres o cuatro. No por la complejidad del contenido, sino por las deficiencias de una herramienta que debería facilitar el proceso creativo, no sabotearlo.

Y lo más grave ni siquiera es eso. En una ocasión, después de dedicar considerable tiempo a estructurar y revisar cuidadosamente un artículo, el resultado publicado apareció con un formato completamente distinto al que había establecido. Al regresar al editor para corregirlo, el contenido seguía mostrando el formato original, como si nada hubiera ocurrido. Una contradicción absurda entre lo que se edita y lo que finalmente se publica.

¿De qué sirve un editor si no garantiza que el resultado publicado respete el trabajo realizado?

Estamos en 2026. Editar un artículo en Substack no debería sentirse como intentar modificar un PDF con herramientas de hace veinte años.

No human support, locked out for 20 days with zero reason.
reviews.text:
My account has been blocked for 20 days and counting. Substack has not provided a single valid explanation. There is no customer service – only an AI chatbot that goes in circles and says nothing helpful.

They have not even sent an email explaining why I was blocked. I have no violation notice, no warning, and no way to appeal. For a platform that takes a cut of writer's money, this is unacceptable. Do not trust them with your livelihood.

reviews.title: Worsening ux
reviews.text: I used to be able to see lots of articles at once and roughly how long each article is, no more. Now i see a giant graphic for each article and only two or three fit on my screen at a time, and you have no way of changing that appearance. I also used to be able to manage a queue of episodes to be read aloud, i just long pressed on an article and i could add it. Now there’s a queue with no obvious way to add to it from the increasingly ugly list of articles, and if i try to manage it i invariably accidentally start playing a thing i already listened to because that’s what send to add itself to my queue. Maybe my favorite is this stupid view that pops up when an article starts playing. It adds no meaningful ui, and when you do a home swipe it messes with the scrubber. Oh, and your voice over skip quotes for some reason. I actually want to read the quote the author put in the article.

The fact you need my phone number and a bunch of other stuff is just ridiculous.

reviews.title: Privacy issues
reviews.text:
When trying to log in to Substack via the app, it asks for many more permissions than if you are using Substack on desktop. One of these is your phone number, which you MUST enter and which the app claims is for security purposes. After the number is entered, you can't remove it from your account—ever. The next screen after entering your number provides the option to share your contacts. I declined this, so I was shocked that on the next screen, it showed me multiple people I know IRL anyway. How did it make this connection? A quick search explained: because THOSE people shared their contacts with Substack, and because my phone number is now irrevocably tied to my account, even though I didn't consent to find or be found through contacts, thanks to someone else opting me in, I don't have a choice.

I don't love giving out my number for 2FA purposes, but it's something I've grudgingly come to accept about using the internet in the modern world. But this is unacceptable. I am even more disgusted because I know it doesn't matter even if I delete my account and request Substack purge my data. They've still got it through other people's accounts, and Substack knows who I know IRL whether I've consented to it or not. And even if you're not a Substack user, even if you're one of those ones who's boycotting them for one reason or other, guess what? They've probably got your data, too, because someone who has your phone number in their contacts has opted you in without your consent.
